newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Zinc price drops almost 20 pct in an hour.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Zinc price drops almost 20 pct in an hour.

text.p: A speculative bubble in the price of zinc collapsed on Tuesday and it sank almost 20 percent in about an hour as investors fled for cover.
Confusion reigned in a market that began to doubt how much more buying of the metal would come from China, seen as the key to the explosive rally of recent weeks.
"We're now in a limbo period...uncertainty pervails until the air clears," said metals analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton.

The key three-month price dropped about $300 to a low of $1,370 per tonne, erasing gains of the past month in the space of an hour as banks, investment funds and other speculators scrambled to liquidate positions.
On Monday, prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) had risen to a seven-year peak of $1,675.
"The market was way over-extended. It was inevitable that we would have some sort of meltdown but the speed and extent has certainly taken people by surprise," MacMillan said.
A trader said: "There was the perception that the market had run out of steam. All volume selling was one-way and there were no buyers, which accounts for the speed of the fall."
Waves of speculative buying swept the market in recent weeks on a bet that Chinese smelters still had massive buying to do after a gamble turned sour.
Chinese officials said recently their smelters had over-extended themselves, agreeing last year to sell up to 250,000 tonnes more than they could produce.
They thought they could make a profit due to falling prices, but instead prices shot up, analysts said. At Monday's peak, prices this year had gained nearly 60 percent.
Traders on the frenzied LME floor on Tuesday morning reckoned the Chinese had completed covering their positions.

On Monday, a senior Chinese industry source said between a half and two-thirds of the Zhuzhou smelter's estimated 90,000 tonnes of short positions had already been covered. But on Tuesday, a Chinese smelter official told Reuters in Shanghai that the "short" position was still intact.
"I can't really say what our position is but it is still there," the source said.
During LME ring trading, spreads contracted but did not collapse, indicating that the market was still affected by shortages for certain dates.
The premium of cash metal to three months material was bid at $50 to $65 after hitting $92 on Monday.
Analysts said three month prices should find support at around $1,400.

"Now that we have had a correction we would expect the price to start picking up again. Funds which have taken profits this morning will look for a better offer," said Adam Rowley of Macquarie Equities.
During LME morning prices recovered to $1,480.
